name: Diego Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Diego, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not funded by AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. So you can tell me the public version and the private version, if they're different.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I talk a lot, so stop me if I go off on one. My partner says I could talk to a brick wall and the wall would end up joining a union.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Ha. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get the 6:10 train into the city, because there's nothing in my trade near where we live, and I'm on an office refurb by quarter past seven. I work for a fit-out firm doing drylining, so metal studs, plasterboard partitions, ceilings, door frames, turning an empty floor into meeting rooms. I was a line cook for twenty years until the restaurant closed in the bad year, so I'm only two years into this and still the slowest on the team. I use the AI on my phone all day, honestly, I photograph the drawing and ask it what the symbols mean so I'm not bothering the foreman every five minutes. What wears me out is the dust and the train home at six with my arms like jelly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it's a great helper but it can't hang a door. I'd probably post a photo of me with a stack of plasterboard and write something like, still waiting for my robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I keep learning the trade the slow way, with the phone as my teacher. Fine by me. But I'd also think, all this money got poured into AI and the guys on my site still haven't had a pay rise in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI to catch up on the stuff the others learned in their apprenticeships, setting-out, reading the fire specs. I'd sign up for the ceiling fixing course the union runs at the training centre. Basically, keep going and get better faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Kind of a shrug, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does it actually do for you on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the drawing had a fire-rated partition with a code I'd never seen, so I asked it, and it told me what boards and how many layers. Then I asked Marek, the foreman, to double-check, and he said I was right and looked a bit annoyed about it. It makes me look less green than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's money like at home right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thin. Ana's a healthcare assistant on night shifts, I'm on the lower rate, and with the mortgage and the train ticket we've got maybe a week or two spare at the end of a month. The train ticket alone is more than our food shop some months.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, it's a great helper but it can't hang a door. I'd post a photo of me with a stack of plasterboard and write, still waiting for my robot.
S0.think: I'd keep learning the trade the slow way, with my phone as my teacher, which is fine. But all that money poured into AI and the guys on my site still haven't had a pay rise in two years.
S0.do: Keeps using AI on his phone to catch up on setting-out and fire specifications, and signs up for the union's ceiling fixing course at the training centre. Carries on with the fit-out firm and tries to improve faster.
S0.feel: Calm, more of a shrug than anything.
S0.quote: Then I asked Marek, the foreman, to double-check, and he said I was right and looked a bit annoyed about it.
S0.fieldNote: He uses AI as a private tutor to make up for coming late to the trade, which is unusual for a junior site worker. Even when nothing changes, he points at who got the money from AI. His money is very thin, and the cost of commuting to the only work available stands out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers get a piece of it. If a machine makes the job quicker, the hours should get shorter or the pay higher, not the crew smaller. I'd say that at the union meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do all right. I'm already the one who knows the apps, and when the new kit turns up, someone has to learn it first. I'd rather be that guy than the guy it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm straight away if I can be trained on whatever new tools come in, the board-lifting machines, the laser layout stuff. I'd do online courses in the evenings, the free ones, after the kids are in bed. And I'd help the older guys use their phones, because if they get left behind the whole crew gets weaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Like when a new menu came in at the restaurant, stressful for a month and then you're faster than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What new jobs do you think might appear on a site like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone to run and fix the machines, someone to check the robot did the partition right before the client sees it. Someone to plan the work so the machines and people aren't in each other's way. I could see myself doing that last one, I've run a kitchen on a Saturday night, I know how to keep five people from colliding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound quite cheerful. Is there anything here that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. Courses and new kit sound great, but if the firm wants me to learn on my own time, that's time I'm not doing weekend jobs. And Ana's on nights, so somebody has to be home with Lucas and Sofia.

S1.say: This is the moment to make sure workers get a piece of it. If a machine makes the job quicker, the hours should get shorter or the pay higher, not the crew smaller.
S1.think: I think I'd do all right, because I'm already the one who knows the apps. When the new kit turns up, someone has to learn it first, and I'd rather be that guy than the guy it replaces.
S1.do: Asks the firm right away to train him on new tools such as board-lifting machines and laser layout, and does free online courses in the evenings. Helps older colleagues use their phones so the crew doesn't get left behind.
S1.feel: Mostly good, like the stress of a new menu that leaves you faster after a month.
S1.quote: I've run a kitchen on a Saturday night, I know how to keep five people from colliding.
S1.fieldNote: He sees the steady picture as an opening and quickly connects his kitchen experience to new site roles. His politics show up as wanting the gains shared through shorter hours or higher pay. The only worry he named was money and childcare, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not a law of nature. Somebody owns the robots, so we should be talking about who owns them and who gets the money. I'd be saying robots should belong to the people whose jobs they take, co-ops, public ownership, something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. Being quick with an app doesn't save you if the app can do the whole job. And I've got no savings to ride it out while I figure out the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get in with whoever is installing the robots, the companies that set them up on site, because they'll need people at first. I'd do weekend jobs for cash, fixing doors, putting up shelves, while there are still people paying for that. And I'd be at every union and community meeting, because this needs to be fought together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like running for a train that's already pulling away. You can see it, you're sprinting, and you know you probably won't make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right in the slower picture. What changes with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'd be jumping before I'm ready. With the slower picture, I could learn the new kit while I'm still being paid. With two years, I'm going from line cook to dryliner to whatever comes next in four years total, with a mortgage on my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would money come from in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend jobs, a bit of help from Ana's brother who has a shop, and whatever the government puts in place, if it does. I'd hate asking for help, but I'm not proud enough to let the kids go without.

S2.say: This is a choice, not a law of nature. Somebody owns the robots, so we should be asking who owns them and who gets the money, through co-ops or public ownership.
S2.think: I'm scared. Being quick with an app doesn't save you if the app can do the whole job, and I've got no savings to ride it out while I work out the next thing.
S2.do: Tries to get hired by the companies installing robots on sites, and does weekend handyman jobs for cash while there's still demand. Goes to every union and community meeting and leans on family and any government help if needed.
S2.feel: Like sprinting for a train that's already pulling away and knowing he probably won't make it.
S2.quote: Like running for a train that's already pulling away. You can see it, you're sprinting, and you know you probably won't make it.
S2.fieldNote: His confidence drops sharply once the timeline shrinks, because being adaptable doesn't help without savings to bridge the gap. His instinct is still to move early, chasing jobs installing the robots. Ownership of the machines is where his politics land when things get serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start today. I'd be pushing the union to set up a training fund and a jobs list, and pushing the politicians to tax the robot firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me a real chance. I could get from beginner dryliner to someone who runs or checks the machines, if I start now and don't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask my firm to put me forward for any robot or automation training, and I'd do the evening courses on site machinery and the free AI courses. I'd try to save fifty a month, even if it's just the train money from the days I cycle. I'd keep the union pushing for a training fund that pays people while they learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd have something to do with the nerves, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you start doing now, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, get trained on whatever the firm brings in. Years two and three, try to move into setting up or checking the machines, even if it means moving firms. By year four, I want to be someone they need, not someone they're paying off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to be curious and stay kind, because those are the things machines are worst at. And I'd tell Lucas that his dad was a cook and a builder and will be something else again, and that's okay. Changing isn't failing.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if we start today. The union should set up a training fund and a jobs list, and the politicians should tax the robot firms.
S3.think: Five years gives me a real chance. If I start now and don't stop, I could go from beginner dryliner to someone who runs or checks the machines.
S3.do: Asks his firm to put him forward for automation training this year and takes evening and free online courses on site machinery and AI. Saves 50 a month by cycling some days, and keeps pushing the union for a paid training fund.
S3.feel: Nervous, but with something useful to do with the nerves.
S3.quote: And I'd tell Lucas that his dad was a cook and a builder and will be something else again, and that's okay. Changing isn't failing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets his adaptability work again, and he set out a clear year-by-year plan. Saving even a little is hard, and his only lever is cycling instead of taking the train. What he would tell his son shows he sees changing careers as normal rather than shameful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to build something fair. Shorter working weeks, retraining paid by the companies, and a real say for workers in how the machines get used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels manageable. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, and I'd have had time to get properly good at something new. I still worry about the guys on my crew who won't change, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first few years getting fully qualified in drylining, because a good tradesman can supervise machines better than a beginner. Then I'd retrain into machine setup or checking, and keep using AI tools every day to stay sharp. I'd campaign for a shorter working week and vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like something I can steer instead of something that just runs me over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there anything you'd hold off on, rather than starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't rush out of drylining. With ten years, I'd rather become properly good at the trade first, because the robots will need people who know what a good wall looks like. I'd hold off on paying for any expensive course until I see which ones lead to real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this that you'd actually welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the machines do the heavy lifting and the dust and we all work four days instead of five. I'd get to see Ana on a weekday, imagine that. But only if the money gets shared, otherwise it's just a nicer-sounding layoff.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so let's use it to build something fair. That means shorter working weeks, retraining paid by the companies, and a real say for workers.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable, with the kids grown and time to get properly good at something new. I still worry about the guys on my crew who won't change.
S4.do: Spends the first years getting fully qualified in drylining, then retrains into setting up or checking site machines. Keeps using AI tools daily and campaigns and votes for a shorter working week.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, as if he can steer this instead of being run over.
S4.quote: But only if the money gets shared, otherwise it's just a nicer-sounding layoff.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, he chooses to deepen his trade first, reasoning that machines will need people who know good work. He can picture a future he'd welcome, but only with shared gains. His concern for less adaptable colleagues comes up again and again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because being quick on my feet doesn't matter if I can't afford to stop and learn. What would help is being paid while I retrain, and some say over the robots, like workers owning a share of them. Even just a guarantee you won't lose the house while you're changing over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the commute. If I lose the city job, there's nothing near home, so I'd be paying for a train to a job that doesn't exist. Nobody plans for the people who live where the work isn't.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans for the people who live where the work isn't.
portrait: Diego is a 43-year-old junior dryliner on city office refurbishments, who switched from twenty years as a line cook two years ago and commutes by train because there's no work near home. He uses AI every day as a private tutor and wants to be the first on his crew to learn new machines. He is calm in the plateau and steady pictures, but alarmed by AGI in two years, because adaptability can't help without savings to bridge the gap. With five or ten years he makes concrete plans to move into setting up or checking machines. His politics centre on who owns the robots and whether the gains are shared.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because being quick to adapt doesn't help if he can't afford to stop working and learn.
whatWouldHelp: Being paid while he retrains, workers owning a share of the robots, and a guarantee he won't lose the house during the change.
